subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 9-year-old boy is evaluated for recurrent episodes of severe epigastric pain. He has eruptive, pruritic yellow papules over the buttocks and extensor surfaces. Fasting triglycerides are 2800 mg/dL, total cholesterol is 410 mg/dL, and a refrigerated serum sample shows a creamy supernatant. Serum amylase and lipase are elevated, and there is no family history of early myocardial infarction.
question: Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect in this patient?

options.text: Deficiency of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein

explanation_correct: Familial hyperchylomicronemia (type I dyslipidemia) results from deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or of its activator apolipoprotein C-II, so chylomicrons and triglycerides accumulate in plasma. The creamy supernatant on refrigerated serum reflects the chylomicron layer, and the marked hypertriglyceridemia causes eruptive xanthomas and acute pancreatitis without accelerated atherosclerosis because LDL is not elevated.

explanation_incorrect.A: Apolipoprotein B-100 is required for VLDL and LDL formation; its absence lowers rather than raises plasma lipids.
explanation_incorrect.C: Defective LDL receptors cause familial hypercholesterolemia with high LDL, tendon xanthomas, and premature coronary disease rather than massive hypertriglyceridemia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Absence of apolipoprotein E (type III dysbetalipoproteinemia) raises remnant particles and produces palmar xanthomas, not a creamy chylomicron layer.
explanation_incorrect.E: Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein deficiency causes abetalipoproteinemia with very low cholesterol and triglycerides, not severe hypertriglyceridemia.

educationalObjective: Type I familial hyperchylomicronemia is caused by lipoprotein lipase or apolipoprotein C-II deficiency and produces severe hypertriglyceridemia, eruptive xanthomas, and pancreatitis without accelerated atherosclerosis.
